Chapter Two

The house on the point had been empty for three winters when the sisters came back to it, and the damp had got into everything that could not be carried away. The wallpaper in the front room hung in long pale tongues, and the piano, which nobody had been strong enough to move, had swollen until its lid would not close over the keys.

Ruth went through the rooms opening windows while her sister stood in the hall with the key still in her hand.

It was Ruth who found the letters. They were in the drawer of the hall table, under a layer of old gloves and seed packets, tied with the green string their mother had used for everything from parcels to the runner beans, and there were more of them than either sister could have guessed. Every one had been opened, and every one had been put back in its envelope with care.

“Leave them,” said her sister from the doorway. “Whatever is in them has waited this long.”
